title: Highest and best use: what a site can legally, physically and financially become
summary: A site is worth what its best permitted and buildable use can pay for it, not what the seller asks. This lesson teaches the four tests of highest and best use, the residual land value screen, and the four desk diligence streams that check both before you spend real money.
body:
Mr Shabazz, you do not buy land; you buy the best building that land is allowed to carry, minus everything it costs to get there. Highest and best use tells you what that building is, and desk diligence tells you whether the story survives contact with the evidence.

Recall

Q. What does title insurance protect against that a title search alone does not?

A. Losses from defects the search missed or could not reveal, such as a forged transfer in the chain, up to the policy limit and subject to the listed exceptions. The search tells you what the record shows; the policy pays when the record was wrong.

Q. How is revenue per available room calculated for a hotel?

A. Average daily rate multiplied by occupancy. A hotel at 150 dollars a night and 70 percent occupancy earns 105 dollars per available room per night, hypothetically.

Q. Name the four places tax touches a real estate deal on the tax map.

A. Transfer taxes on the way in, value-added or goods and services tax on supplies, tax on gains on the way out, and recapture of depreciation already claimed.

Why this matters

Every bad land deal I have seen starts the same way: somebody falls in love with a building before proving the land can hold it. The asking price is anchored to a hope, the buyer anchors to the asking price, and three months later the geotechnical report, the zoning by-law or the environmental search says the hope was never available. When you run your own projects there is no head office to catch that. The discipline in this lesson is what stands between you and paying full price for a building you are not allowed, or cannot afford, to build.

The four tests, in order

Plain English first. Highest and best use asks one question: of all the things this site could become, which one produces the most value? Appraisers answer it with four tests applied in a fixed order, and the order is the point.

  1. Legally permissible. What does zoning, title and any registered agreement allow today, and what could realistically be approved? A use that needs a rezoning is not dead, but it carries entitlement risk and must be priced that way.
  2. Physically possible. Can the ground, the shape of the lot, the access, the flood level and the servicing actually support it? A permitted twelve-storey tower on soft ground with no sewer capacity is permitted and impossible.
  3. Financially feasible. Does the completed value exceed the total cost, including a return the market demands? Many uses pass the first two tests and fail here.
  4. Maximally productive. Of the uses that pass all three, which yields the highest land value? That one is the highest and best use.

The professional framing: the appraisal profession treats highest and best use as the foundation of every valuation, and it is analysed both "as vacant" and "as improved" when a building already stands. Notice what the order does. It stops you running financial models on fantasies. You filter by law and physics first, so every number you compute afterwards is about a building that can exist.

Applied example, hypothetical numbers. A 2,000 square metre lot is zoned for residential use up to four storeys. You sketch three options: 12 townhouses, a 40-unit four-storey apartment building, and a 90-unit tower. The tower fails the legal test, so it is out unless you choose to fight for a rezoning. Desk research shows a high water table, so a full basement car park under the apartment building is physically possible but costly. Both remaining options go to the financial test, and the winner is whichever leaves the most money for the land.

Residual land value: the land is what is left

Here is the idea that changes how you look at every listing. Start with what the finished project is worth. Subtract every cost of building it, the interest, the fees, and the profit a developer must earn to take the risk. What is left is the most a rational developer can pay for the land. That number is the residual land value.

The formula, said aloud: residual land value equals gross development value, minus total development cost excluding land, minus required developer profit. Gross development value means the completed project's sale value or capitalised value.

Applied example, hypothetical round numbers. The 40-unit building sells for 400,000 dollars a unit, so gross development value is 16 million dollars. Hard costs, soft costs, finance costs and contingency come to 11 million. The market requires a developer profit of 15 percent of value, which is 2.4 million. Sixteen million minus 11 million minus 2.4 million leaves 2.6 million. Now run the townhouses: 12 units at 650,000 dollars is 7.8 million of value, costs of 5.2 million, profit of 1.17 million, leaving about 1.43 million. The apartment building supports nearly twice the land value, so it is the highest and best use, provided its costs are real. The required profit margin here is commercial practice, not a standard; markets and lenders move it.

Say that out loud now.

Residual land value equals value, minus cost, minus profit. If the seller asks more than that number, the seller is asking you to give them your profit.

Desk diligence: four streams before boots on the ground

Diligence means the investigation a careful buyer carries out before committing. Desk diligence is the part done from records, maps and documents before you pay for drilling, sampling or detailed design. It is cheap, fast and kills most bad deals. Cole, our auditor, insists on one principle: every finding needs a source you can produce later.

  • Legal. Title, registered easements and encumbrances, zoning and official plan designation, any development agreement already on title, outstanding work orders, leases or occupants, and litigation searches against the owner.
  • Tax. How the purchase will be taxed on the way in, whether the seller's status creates obligations for you as buyer, the property tax history and assessed value, and whether indirect tax applies to the sale. Verify each point against the primary source before you rely on it.
  • Environmental. Historical uses of the site and its neighbours from records, maps and aerial photographs. In the United States the common screening document is a Phase I environmental site assessment prepared to an ASTM standard; verify against the current edition. A Phase I flags concerns; it does not prove the ground is clean.
  • Geotechnical. Published geological maps, nearby borehole records, flood mapping, previous fill, slopes and groundwater. This is a desk study, not a design. It tells you whether to budget for ordinary foundations or something expensive.

Applied example: the desk geotechnical study on our hypothetical lot finds a filled former creek bed across one corner. That single line moves the apartment building's foundation allowance, which moves the residual land value, which moves the price you can offer. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineering, before any of that becomes a design number.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is reversing the order: deciding the building first and then reading the diligence to confirm it. That is confirmation bias wearing a hard hat. The control is a written screen completed before any offer: the four tests in order, each stream's finding with its source, and the residual land value calculated at the downside cost, not the hoped-for cost. If the asking price exceeds the downside residual, you either negotiate with conditions or you walk.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner starts from the asking price and asks, "Can I make it work?" Almost anything can be made to work on a spreadsheet by squeezing contingency and inflating rents. The professional starts from the building, works backward to the land, and treats the asking price as the seller's opening opinion, nothing more.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the purchase structure decides transfer tax and future treatment of gains; settle it before you sign, and verify against the primary source. Liability: environmental liability can attach to an owner who did not cause the contamination, so diligence findings decide what you are inheriting. Banking: a lender will repeat your diligence; weak findings become loan conditions or a lower loan. Governance: record who approved the go decision and on what evidence. Estate: land held for years becomes part of an estate, so the holding entity matters from day one. Exit: the buyer you sell to will run the same four tests; an unresolved finding becomes their discount.

Callback

In Week 28 you learned the go/no-go gate in feasibility: absorption as a number, competing supply and a decision you write down before you are emotionally invested. Highest and best use is the land-side twin of that gate. Feasibility asks whether the market wants the building; highest and best use asks whether this land can deliver it. You need both answers yes before you sign anything binding.

Recap

Filter uses by law, then physics, then money, then pick the most productive. Calculate residual land value as value minus cost minus profit, and treat it as your ceiling. Run legal, tax, environmental and geotechnical desk diligence first, with a source for every finding. Next: Ford takes us through Failure Forensics on a tower that settled, and what diligence must ask about the ground and the neighbours.
checklist: Apply the four tests in order: legal, physical, financial, maximally productive
Sketch at least two alternative uses before favouring one
Calculate residual land value at downside cost, not hoped-for cost
Treat the asking price as an opinion, not a starting point
Run legal, tax, environmental and geotechnical desk diligence before any field spend
Record a source for every diligence finding
Write the go or no-go decision down before making an offer
Get the geotechnical engineer to confirm any foundation allowance
head: Field checklist
speak: Highest and best use asks what this land can best become. You test it in a fixed order: is it legally permitted, is it physically possible, is it financially feasible, and of what survives, which is most productive. The order stops you modelling buildings that cannot exist. Then you work out residual land value: what the finished project is worth, minus every cost of building it, minus the profit a developer needs to take the risk. What is left is the most you can rationally pay. If the seller asks more, they are asking for your profit. Before you spend money in the field, run four desk streams: legal, tax, environmental and geotechnical, each finding with a source. The biggest risk is choosing the building first and reading the diligence to confirm it. So write the screen down, price at the downside cost, and walk if the numbers do not hold.
terms: Highest and best use — the reasonably probable use of a site that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and produces the highest value.
Residual land value — the completed project's value minus all development costs and required profit; the most a rational developer can pay for the land.
Desk diligence — investigation from records, maps and documents done before paying for field work such as drilling or sampling.

hostile.q: Your residual land value supports the asking price only if costs come in at your estimate. Why should I lend against a land value that disappears with a ten percent overrun?
hostile.a: You should not, and I do not ask you to. I calculated the residual at the downside cost case as well as the base case, and my offer is set at the downside number, not the base. The difference is held as conditions in the purchase agreement, and the geotechnical desk study has already been reflected in the foundation allowance. If field investigation moves the cost further, the conditional period lets me renegotiate or walk before the deposit is at risk.

role: Failure forensics (with Cole, audit and integrity)
title: Millennium Tower: when the ground and the neighbours are part of the deal
summary: A San Francisco residential tower completed in 2009 was reported in 2016 to have settled and tilted, triggering years of litigation and a costly retrofit. Ford takes it through seven steps to show what site diligence must ask about the ground's long-term behaviour and about what the neighbours plan to dig.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a building can be designed to a recognised approach, approved, built and sold, and still become a decade-long dispute because nobody owned the question of what the ground would do over time and what the site next door would do to it. Diligence is where that question gets owned or orphaned.

Recall

Q. What is a survey's job in the title picture?

A. To show where the boundaries, buildings, easements and encroachments physically sit on the ground, so you can compare the paper title with what is actually there.

Q. Why do hotel and apartment assets carry different risk at the same income?

A. Hotel income is re-earned every night and swings with the economy, while apartment income sits on leases. That is why lenders and buyers usually price hotel income with a higher yield.

Q. What is depreciation recapture?

A. When an asset sells for more than its tax-depreciated value, some or all of the depreciation claimed earlier can be brought back into income. How and at what rate depends on the system; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

You will buy land beside other people's projects. You will rarely drill as deeply or as widely as an engineer would like before you close. This case shows two diligence gaps that a small developer can close cheaply on paper: the ground's long-term movement, and the neighbours' plans. I am working only from public reporting. Where I describe allegations, I say so, because the disputes ended in settlement rather than in a court finding on every point.

The case in seven steps

Step 1, timeline. Millennium Tower is a residential condominium tower of about 58 storeys in San Francisco, completed in 2009. Its foundation was a concrete mat on piles that reached into a dense sand layer rather than down to bedrock, a friction-pile approach. Next door, excavation for the Transbay Transit Center went ahead in the following years. In 2016 it became public that the tower had settled by more than a foot and was tilting. Lawsuits followed among owners, the developer, the transit authority and others, and were largely resolved by settlement around 2020. A perimeter pile retrofit was then undertaken; it was paused when the work itself appeared to accelerate settlement, and resumed in a reduced form.

Step 2, key decisions. The foundation type was chosen during design and accepted through the approval process. The adjacent transit project designed and carried out its own deep excavation and dewatering, meaning pumping groundwater out to keep the excavation dry. Later, the parties chose how and when to disclose observed settlement.

Step 3, assumptions. The predicted settlement for the tower was an assumption about how the sand and the softer clay beneath it would behave under load over decades. A second assumption, built into each project separately, was that the other project's effects were the other project's problem.

Step 4, incentives. A developer is paid on completion and sale; a foundation to bedrock costs more and takes longer. A public transit project is judged on its own schedule and budget. Neither incentive is wicked. Both point away from spending money on the interaction between two sites.

Step 5, warning signs ignored. Public reporting and the lawsuits alleged that settlement greater than predicted was observed before it was disclosed to buyers. Those allegations were contested, and I cannot tell you a court found them true. What I can tell you is the generic warning sign: monitoring data that runs ahead of the prediction is information, and information that is not escalated becomes liability.

Step 6, point of no return. Once the tower was built and the units sold, the foundation could only be fixed by working under and around an occupied building, which is slow, uncertain and very expensive. The cheap decision point was before the foundation was designed, when the ground's long-term behaviour and the neighbour's planned excavation could have been put in one risk register.

Step 7, root cause. Not one bad engineer. The root cause was a boundary problem: the risk sat between two sites, two owners and two sets of consultants, and no single party was paid to own the interaction.

Say that out loud now.

The risk that sits between two parties belongs to nobody until you make it yours.

Worked example one: the neighbour search

Hypothetical. You are looking at a lot beside a vacant parcel. Your desk diligence adds one line that most buyers skip: search the planning and permit records for the adjacent parcels. You find an approved application next door for a building with two levels of underground parking. That tells you to ask three things in writing: will they dewater, what monitoring will they install, and who carries the cost if your building moves. You put an allowance of, say, 150,000 dollars for monitoring and protective measures into your budget, hypothetically, and you require your geotechnical engineer to comment on the interaction. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineering.

Worked example two: what settlement costs the pro forma

Hypothetical round numbers. A 40-unit building with a gross development value of 16 million dollars. Suppose a settlement dispute delays the last 10 sales by 18 months and requires a 5 percent price cut to clear them. Ten units at 400,000 dollars is 4 million; a 5 percent cut costs 200,000 dollars. Carrying 4 million of unsold stock for 18 months at a hypothetical 8 percent cost of money is roughly 480,000 dollars. Add legal fees and the developer's time and you have well over 700,000 dollars of damage from a problem that a 150,000 dollar line in diligence might have shaped. The numbers are invented; the asymmetry is the lesson.

Cole's audit note

Cole would read the file like this: where is the record that the foundation choice considered adjacent excavation, where is the monitoring plan, and where is the escalation rule that says what happens when readings exceed prediction? If those three documents do not exist, the risk was never owned. Write them early and they cost almost nothing.

Cole would add a second question, about evidence. Suppose your building does move. Your neighbour's engineer will say the movement was always going to happen; yours will say the excavation caused it. The side with a baseline wins that argument: dated photographs of every crack before work starts, survey points read on a fixed schedule, and groundwater levels logged. Without a baseline, cause becomes an opinion contest, and opinion contests are settled by whoever can afford to keep paying experts. A baseline condition survey on a small building is a modest fee. It is one of the best-value documents in development, and it only works if it exists before the first shovel goes in next door.

The biggest risk

Treating your site as an island. Ground, groundwater, drainage and vibration do not respect a property line. The control: every site file contains a neighbours' section listing adjacent approvals and planned works, a monitoring and escalation plan for any construction next door, and a contractual position on who pays for movement.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that approval means safety. A permit says the design met the requirements the authority checked. It does not say the long-term behaviour of the ground was the conservative case, and it says nothing about what your neighbour will do next year.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema and I taught the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and write down why. Run that exercise here and "the building next door dug a hole" appears in the first five minutes. A pre-mortem is free; this case shows what it costs to skip it.

Recap

The tower's problems came from a risk that sat between two projects and two incentives, with monitoring data and disclosure in dispute. Your controls are cheap: search the neighbours, plan monitoring, set an escalation rule, and allocate the cost of movement in writing. Rule 31 below is the one to keep. Next: Roman on The Money, what each diligence finding does to value and to the loan.
checklist: Search planning and permit records for every adjacent parcel
Ask in writing whether neighbours will excavate or dewater
Have the geotechnical engineer comment on long-term settlement and adjacent works
Put a monitoring and protective-works allowance in the budget
Set an escalation rule for monitoring readings above prediction
Allocate the cost of ground movement in writing
Record when and how any adverse finding is disclosed
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 31: Know what is under the ground and what will be dug next to it before you own the site, and give the risk between two sites a named owner in writing.
speak: Millennium Tower in San Francisco was completed in 2009 on piles that reached a sand layer rather than bedrock. In 2016 it became public that it had settled more than a foot and was tilting. Next door, a transit centre had dug a deep excavation. Lawsuits followed and were largely settled around 2020, and a retrofit followed that itself ran into trouble. The allegations about who knew what and when were contested, so I will not tell you a court found them. What matters to you is the root cause: the risk sat between two sites and two owners, and nobody was paid to own the interaction. Your controls are cheap. Search the permit records of every neighbour. Ask whether they will dig or pump groundwater. Get your geotechnical engineer to comment on long-term settlement. Budget monitoring. Write down who pays if your building moves. Rule 31: know what is under the ground and what will be dug next to it.
terms: Friction pile — a pile that carries load mainly through friction along its sides in the soil, rather than by bearing on rock at its tip.
Dewatering — pumping groundwater out of or around an excavation to keep it dry, which can lower water levels and move ground nearby.
Settlement — the downward movement of a building as the ground beneath it compresses under load over time.

hostile.q: An investor asks: your site is next to an approved excavation. If your building moves, who pays, and how would you even prove the cause?
hostile.a: Before closing, I have the neighbour's approval on file, a geotechnical comment on the interaction, and a baseline condition survey with monitoring points installed before their work starts. That baseline is how cause gets proven. On cost, the purchase price reflects a monitoring allowance, and I am seeking a written arrangement with the neighbour on monitoring access and responsibility. If I cannot get that, the risk is priced in the land offer, not left to argue about later.

title: Diligence as a priced option: turning findings into price, reserve or walk
summary: Every diligence dollar buys the right to change your mind before the money is at risk. Roman shows how to size diligence spend against value at risk, how each finding becomes a price cut, a reserve or a walk, and how a lender re-reads the same file.
body:
Mr Shabazz, diligence is not a cost of buying land; it is the price of an option to walk away. The question is never "how little can I spend?" but "what is the information worth compared with the money it protects?"

Recall

Q. When an easement crosses the only sensible building footprint, what are your commercial options before closing?

A. Negotiate its release or relocation with the holder, redesign around it, reprice the land to reflect the lost value, or walk away during the conditional period. Which one depends on cost and on whether the holder will deal.

Q. What does gross operating profit measure in a hotel?

A. Total hotel revenue minus the departmental and undistributed operating expenses, before management fees, fixed charges and capital items. It shows how well the operation converts revenue into profit.

Q. Why is a land transfer tax a development cost and not just a closing fee?

A. Because it is cash out on day one that the project must recover through value. It belongs in sources and uses and it lowers the residual land value you can pay.

Why this matters

A grid operator runs N-minus-1: the system must survive the loss of any single element. Diligence is N-minus-1 for a land purchase. You pay a little before closing so that the loss of any single assumption, clean soil, buildable ground, clear title, does not take the whole project down. A small developer who skips diligence to save 40,000 dollars is self-insuring a risk worth millions without writing the policy down.

Diligence is an option you buy

Plain English: a conditional offer gives you a period in which you may walk away. Each report you commission during that period buys information that might tell you to walk. The cost of the report is the option premium.

Professional framing: you weigh the cost of information against the expected loss it lets you avoid. Expected loss means the probability of a problem multiplied by the cost of that problem if you only find it after closing.

Worked example one, hypothetical numbers. A site was a vehicle repair shop for 20 years. The Phase I environmental site assessment, a records-based screen, flags possible underground tanks. A Phase II, meaning actual sampling of soil and groundwater, costs 35,000 dollars. Your environmental consultant's judgement, which is a practitioner estimate not a statistic, is that there is a meaningful chance, say one in four, of contamination needing remediation costing around 600,000 dollars. Expected loss is 0.25 times 600,000, which is 150,000 dollars. You are being offered a 35,000 dollar option to avoid a 150,000 dollar expected loss and a possible 600,000 dollar actual one. Buy the option.

Now flip it. If the site was always a grass field, the chance might be tiny and the Phase II would buy almost nothing. Same report, different value. That is why diligence scope follows history, not habit.

Findings become numbers: price, reserve or walk

Every adverse finding has exactly three commercial outcomes. You reprice the land, you hold back money in a reserve, or you walk. Doing nothing is not a fourth option; it is choosing to absorb the cost silently.

  • Reprice when the cost is known and bounded, for example a measured quantity of contaminated soil to remove.
  • Reserve or holdback when the cost is uncertain but capped: part of the price sits in escrow, meaning held by a neutral party, until the work is done, and is released to the seller only if the cost comes in under it.
  • Walk when the cost is unbounded, the liability cannot be contained, or the finding kills the highest and best use.

Say that out loud now.

Every finding becomes a price, a reserve or a walk. Silence is choosing to pay for it yourself.

Worked example two, hypothetical numbers. The Phase II finds hydrocarbon contamination around the old tanks. The consultant estimates remediation at 400,000 to 700,000 dollars. You offered 2.6 million. Your counter: price reduced by the low estimate to 2.2 million, plus a 300,000 dollar holdback in escrow covering the gap to the high estimate, released to the seller to the extent remediation comes in under 700,000. The seller is paid for clean land, and you are not paying for dirty land at a clean price. Professional sign-off required: environmental engineering and a lawyer for the escrow terms.

What the lender does with your file

A construction lender will not trust your conclusions; it will read your reports, often commission its own, and turn every open item into a condition precedent, meaning something that must be satisfied before the loan funds. Three effects hit your returns directly.

  1. Lower land value in the loan. Lenders commonly credit land at the lower of cost and appraised value. If the appraiser marks the land down for contamination, your equity credit shrinks.
  2. Bigger contingency. Ground and environmental uncertainty usually means the lender demands more contingency, which is more equity from you.
  3. Slower first draw. Unresolved findings delay funding, and every month of delay is interest on the land and your overhead.

Hypothetical: on a 14 million dollar total cost, a lender lending 65 percent of cost advances 9.1 million. If it raises contingency by 300,000 dollars and keeps the same loan, your equity rises by 300,000. Loan-to-cost limits like 65 percent are commercial practice, not a standard; they vary by lender and cycle. Good diligence done early means you hand the lender clean answers and keep that money in your pocket.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet: a land deposit is the most illiquid money you own until the conditions are waived. Count it as at risk, not as an asset you can draw on. And an environmental liability you inherit can follow the owner, which may be you personally if the land is not held in a separate entity. The structure decision belongs before closing; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

Running out of conditional period before the findings are priced. Reports arrive late, the deadline arrives on time, and you waive conditions to avoid losing the deal. The control: a diligence schedule built backward from the waiver date, with every report ordered on day one and a hard rule that an unpriced finding means you ask for an extension or you walk.

The beginner's mistake

Treating diligence as a list of reports to collect rather than questions to answer. A beginner says, "I have the Phase I." A professional says, "The Phase I raised two concerns, here is what each costs, and here is how the offer reflects them."

Working with advisers

Diligence is where you will hire the most advisers in the shortest time, and the temptation is to let each one define their own scope. Do not. Write the question you need answered, the decision it feeds and the date, and send that to the consultant. A report that answers the consultant's standard scope but not your decision is an invoice, not information.

Then read every report for its limitations section first. That is where the adviser tells you what they did not do. The gap between what you assumed they checked and what they actually checked is where the expensive surprises live.

Callback

In Week 13 you built sources and uses and learned contingency by estimate class. Diligence findings are how a Class 5 guess on site costs becomes a Class 3 number. Every report that narrows a range should shrink contingency in the pro forma and show up in the residual land value.

Recap

Size diligence against expected loss, not against habit. Convert every finding into a price cut, a reserve or a walk. Expect the lender to reread everything and charge you for whatever is left open. Next: LEX on The Rules, what the law makes the buyer responsible for finding, and a comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach it.
checklist: Order every diligence report on day one of the conditional period
Build the diligence schedule backward from the condition waiver date
Estimate expected loss before deciding whether to buy a report
Convert each adverse finding into a price cut, reserve or walk
Write each consultant's scope as a question tied to a decision and a date
Read each report's limitations section first
Hand the lender clean answers before it asks
Hold the deposit as at-risk money until conditions are waived
head: Field checklist
speak: Diligence is the price of an option to walk away. You compare what a report costs with the expected loss it helps you avoid: the chance of a problem times what that problem costs if you find it after closing. A 35,000 dollar soil sampling study on an old repair shop is cheap if there is a real chance of a 600,000 dollar clean-up. On a grass field it buys almost nothing. Every adverse finding has three outcomes: reprice the land when the cost is known, hold back money in escrow when it is uncertain but capped, or walk when it is unbounded. Silence means you pay for it yourself. Expect your lender to reread the file and turn every open item into a condition, a lower land credit or more contingency, all of which come out of your equity. The biggest risk is the deadline arriving before the findings are priced. Build the schedule backward from the waiver date.
terms: Expected loss — the probability of a problem multiplied by its cost; used to judge whether information is worth buying.
Holdback — part of the purchase price held in escrow and released only once a defined cost or condition is resolved.
Condition precedent — something that must be satisfied before an obligation, such as funding a loan, takes effect.

hostile.q: A lender asks: your Phase II shows contamination and you are still buying. Why is this not a liability you are importing into my security?
hostile.a: Because it is measured and ring-fenced. The remediation estimate is a range from the environmental engineer, the low end is taken off the price, and the gap to the high end sits in an escrow holdback funded by the seller's proceeds. The remediation plan is scheduled before vertical construction and you will have the closure report before your first construction draw. The land is held in a single-purpose entity, and my contingency is sized on the high estimate, not the low one.

title: Buyer beware: who the law makes responsible for what you did not find
summary: In most land sales the law starts from buyer beware, so what you do not find you usually own. LEX explains the default, the contract tools that shift it, why a consultant's report may not protect you without reliance, and how Canada and Guyana approach the point conceptually.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the default rule in most land sales is that the buyer takes the land as it is. Diligence is how you find the problems; the purchase contract is how you decide who pays for the ones you miss.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between an easement and an encumbrance?

A. An encumbrance is any interest or claim that burdens title, such as a mortgage, a lien or a restrictive covenant. An easement is one kind of encumbrance: a right for someone else to use your land for a specific purpose, such as access or a utility line.

Q. Why does a condominium carry legal obligations that a rental building does not?

A. Because it creates many separate owners bound by a declaration and a governing statute, with rules on the corporation, common elements, reserve funds and buyer protection. A rental building has one owner and landlord-tenant law instead.

Q. When a deal says "the buyer pays transfer tax", does that bind the tax authority?

A. No. The contract allocates the cost between the parties; the statute decides who the authority can collect from. Verify against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

You will sign purchase agreements drafted by a seller's lawyer whose job is to give you as little protection as possible. If you do not know the default rule, you will not notice what a clause is quietly taking away. This lesson teaches concepts and how to think, not the law of any particular place. Every point here must be verified against the primary source and confirmed by your own lawyer before you rely on it.

The default: buyer beware

Plain English: in the common law tradition the starting point for land is caveat emptor, Latin for "let the buyer beware". The seller generally does not have to point out defects you could have found by inspecting. If you could have looked and did not, the loss is usually yours.

Professional framing: the default bends in recognised ways, and the details vary by jurisdiction. Courts in many places treat active concealment or misrepresentation differently from silence. Some systems recognise a duty to disclose certain hidden, or latent, defects that make the property dangerous or unfit and that the seller knew about. Patent defects, the ones visible on reasonable inspection, rarely give you a claim. And many places have statutes that override the common law for particular issues, environmental contamination being the most important for developers.

Applied example, hypothetical. You buy a lot and later find buried demolition rubble that doubles your foundation cost. If the seller said nothing and a test pit would have found it, you are probably on your own. If the seller wrote in a disclosure that "no fill has been placed on the property" and had a contractor's invoice for placing it, you may have a misrepresentation claim. The difference between those two outcomes is a document. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed where the land sits.

Contract tools that move the risk

Because the default favours the seller, the buyer's protection is written in. Four tools matter most.

  1. Conditions. The deal becomes binding only once you are satisfied with diligence, financing or approvals by a date. A well-drafted condition is in your sole discretion; a badly drafted one requires you to prove the land is unsuitable.
  2. Representations and warranties. Statements of fact by the seller, for example that there are no known environmental orders, no undisclosed leases and no pending litigation. Read whether they survive closing and for how long, and whether they are limited to the seller's knowledge.
  3. Indemnities. A promise to cover a defined loss. An environmental indemnity from a seller with no assets after closing is worth little; pair it with a holdback.
  4. "As is, where is" clauses. The seller's counter-tool. They try to restore buyer beware in full and often add a release of claims. Price that clause; never ignore it.

Say that out loud now.

The law starts with the buyer beware. My contract decides which risks move back to the seller, and my diligence decides which ones I price.

Environmental liability: the statute can reach the owner

Many environmental regimes do not stop at "the polluter pays". They can impose clean-up obligations on current owners or persons in control of a contaminated site, whether or not they caused the contamination. Some offer limited protections for buyers who carried out appropriate inquiry before buying. In the United States, the federal Superfund law includes defences tied to "all appropriate inquiries", and a Phase I assessment to the relevant ASTM standard is the common way buyers try to meet them. Verify the current requirements against the primary source; the standards and rules change.

Applied example, hypothetical. Two buyers each purchase a former repair shop. Buyer A commissioned a Phase I, followed up the recommendations and documented it. Buyer B relied on the seller's word. Both later receive a regulatory order. Buyer A may have a defence or a basis to argue; Buyer B has a cheque to write. Same land, same contamination, different paperwork.

Reliance: whose report is it?

A consultant's report is generally owed to the client who engaged it, under that engagement's terms and liability cap. If you rely on a report the seller commissioned, you may have no contractual claim if it is wrong. A reliance letter is a document in which the consultant agrees that a named third party, such as you or your lender, may rely on the report, usually on the same terms. Lenders routinely demand one. If you cannot get one, budget to commission your own report.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison for orientation only. Verify against primary source before you rely on any of it.

Canada. Land law and environmental regulation are largely provincial, so the answer changes by province, and Quebec follows the civil law tradition rather than common law. Many provinces use a land titles or Torrens-style registry in which the register itself is guaranteed to a significant degree, while some still have registry systems in parts of their territory. Provincial environmental statutes in several provinces can reach current owners and persons in control. The practical consequence: your lawyer and environmental consultant must both be local to the province.

Guyana. My understanding is that Guyana has a common law legal system with a Roman-Dutch heritage still visible in land law, where ownership has traditionally passed by a transport, a conveyance passed before a judge in the Deeds Registry, with a separate land registration system applying in some areas. Environmental regulation sits with a national agency under an environmental protection statute. The practical consequence: confirm which registration system governs the parcel and what searches are possible, because the evidence available to a buyer depends on it.

The thinking point common to both: before you rely on any search, ask what the registry actually guarantees, and what a regulator can require of an owner who did not cause the problem.

The biggest risk

Signing an "as is" agreement with weak conditions and then discovering the problem after waiver. The control: never waive a diligence condition until every stream has reported in writing, the findings are priced, and your lawyer has confirmed what the contract leaves with you.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming a seller's report protects you. It protects the seller's engagement. Get reliance or get your own.

Callback

In Week 20 you learned what binds in a letter of intent and what does not. The same habit applies here: read every clause by asking whose risk it is if this turns out false. Representations, indemnities and "as is" language are risk transfers, and you should be able to say aloud which way each one points.

Recap

The default is buyer beware, bent by misrepresentation, some latent-defect duties and statutes. Conditions, representations, indemnities and holdbacks move risk back; "as is" pushes it forward. Environmental law can reach an innocent owner, and documented inquiry is your best protection. Get reliance on reports. Next: Sage on The Numbers, a full residual land value worked step by step.
checklist: Read the purchase agreement asking whose risk each clause leaves
Draft diligence conditions in your sole discretion with clear dates
Check whether representations survive closing and are knowledge-limited
Pair any seller indemnity with a holdback
Commission or document a Phase I environmental assessment to the current standard
Obtain reliance letters on any report you or your lender will rely on
Confirm which land registration system governs the parcel
Never waive conditions until every finding is priced and reviewed by your lawyer
head: Field checklist
speak: In most land sales the starting rule is buyer beware. If you could have found a defect by looking, the loss is usually yours. The default bends: active concealment and misrepresentation are treated differently, some places require disclosure of known hidden defects, and environmental statutes can make a current owner pay to clean up contamination they did not cause. Because the default favours the seller, your protection has to be written into the contract: conditions you control, representations that survive closing, indemnities backed by a holdback, and a hard look at any as-is clause. A seller's consultant report is owed to the seller; get a reliance letter or commission your own. Canada and Guyana both have common law roots, but the land registries, environmental agencies and searches differ, and in Canada they differ by province. Verify every point against the primary source and a local lawyer before relying on it. Never waive a condition until the findings are priced.
terms: Caveat emptor — let the buyer beware; the default that a buyer takes land as it is and bears defects they could have discovered.
Representation and warranty — a seller's contractual statement of fact that gives the buyer a claim if it proves false, within the limits the contract sets.
Reliance letter — a consultant's written agreement that a named third party may rely on a report, usually on the original engagement's terms.

hostile.q: Opposing counsel says: the agreement is as is, where is, and your client had a full conditional period. Why should the seller carry any environmental exposure after closing?
hostile.a: Because my client did exactly what the agreement anticipated: commissioned a Phase I, followed its recommendations and found contamination the seller's own disclosure said did not exist. My client is not asking the seller to carry unknown risk. We are asking for a price that reflects a measured finding and a capped holdback for the uncertain part. If the seller prefers, we will extend the conditional period for further sampling, but we will not waive on an unpriced finding.

title: Residual land value, line by line, and why the land moves faster than anything else
summary: Sage works a full residual land value calculation for a hypothetical 40-unit building, with units on every line. Then two sensitivity tests show the central fact of land pricing: a small change in cost or price makes a large change in what the land is worth.
body:
Mr Shabazz, land is the last line in the stack, so it absorbs every error above it. A 10 percent cost overrun on the building can wipe out a third of what the land is worth.

Recall

Q. What are the four tests of highest and best use, in order?

A. Legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive. The order filters out impossible buildings before any money is modelled.

Q. A hotel runs at 75 percent occupancy and earns 120 dollars per available room. What is the average daily rate?

A. Revenue per available room divided by occupancy: 120 divided by 0.75 is 160 dollars, hypothetically.

Q. If a transfer tax were 3 percent of price, what does it add to a 2 million dollar land purchase?

A. 60,000 dollars of cash on day one. The rate here is hypothetical; verify the actual rate against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Brokers price land by comparing it with other sales. Developers who survive price land by building the project on paper and seeing what is left. When the two numbers disagree, the residual is telling you something the comparables cannot: what this site, with this building, at today's costs, can actually pay. Every number below is hypothetical and rounded for the ear.

Step one: the building and its value

Plain English: first decide how big the building is and what it sells for.

  1. Units: 40 apartments averaging 80 square metres of saleable area. Saleable area is 40 times 80, which is 3,200 square metres.
  2. Efficiency: saleable area is 80 percent of gross floor area, the rest being corridors, stairs, walls and plant. Gross floor area is 3,200 divided by 0.80, which is 4,000 square metres.
  3. Sale price: 5,000 dollars per square metre of saleable area. Gross development value is 3,200 times 5,000, which is 16,000,000 dollars.
  4. Sales costs: commissions, marketing and legal on sales at 4 percent of value, which is 640,000 dollars.

Notice that sale price applies to saleable area and construction cost applies to gross area. Mixing those two is the most common error in a back-of-envelope residual.

Step two: the cost to build

  1. Hard cost, meaning the physical construction: 2,000 dollars per square metre of gross floor area times 4,000 square metres, which is 8,000,000 dollars.
  2. Soft costs, meaning design, permits, fees, insurance and project management: 15 percent of hard cost, which is 1,200,000 dollars.
  3. Contingency: 5 percent of hard plus soft. Hard plus soft is 9,200,000, so contingency is 460,000 dollars.
  4. Subtotal before finance: 9,660,000 dollars.
  5. Construction finance: a loan covers 65 percent of that subtotal, which is about 6,279,000 dollars. Over a 24-month build the loan is on average about half drawn, so the average balance is about 3,140,000. At a hypothetical 8 percent a year for 2 years, interest is about 502,000 dollars. Call it 500,000.
  6. Total development cost excluding land: 10,160,000 dollars.

The 65 percent and the 8 percent are commercial assumptions, not standards; your lender and the cycle will set the real ones.

Step three: profit, then what is left

The market requires a developer profit for taking the risk. Here we use 15 percent of gross development value, which is 2,400,000 dollars. Again, that margin is commercial practice and varies with risk and cycle.

Now subtract, slowly:

  • Gross development value: 16,000,000.
  • Minus sales costs of 640,000 leaves 15,360,000.
  • Minus total development cost of 10,160,000 leaves 5,200,000.
  • Minus required profit of 2,400,000 leaves 2,800,000 dollars.

That 2,800,000 must pay for the land and the cost of acquiring it. If acquisition costs, transfer tax and legal fees together, are a hypothetical 3 percent of the land price, then land times 1.03 equals 2,800,000. Land equals 2,800,000 divided by 1.03, which is about 2,718,000 dollars. Residual land value: roughly 2.72 million.

One simplification to state aloud: we funded the land with equity and treated the cost of that equity as part of the required profit. If you borrow for the land, add the land loan interest as a cost and the residual falls.

Say that out loud now.

Value 16 million, minus sales costs, minus 10.16 million to build, minus 2.4 million profit, leaves 2.8 million. Take out acquisition costs and the land is worth about 2.72 million.

Step four: the sensitivity that matters

Test one, costs up 10 percent. Hard cost rises 800,000, soft cost rises 120,000, contingency rises 46,000 and interest rises roughly 50,000. Total development cost rises by about 1,018,000 dollars. The 2,800,000 left for land falls to about 1,782,000, and land value falls to about 1,730,000. A 10 percent cost move cut the land value by roughly 36 percent.

Test two, sale price down 5 percent. Value falls 800,000 to 15,200,000. Sales costs fall 32,000 and required profit falls 120,000 because profit is a percentage of value. Net, the amount left for land falls by 648,000 to 2,152,000, and land value falls to about 2,089,000. A 5 percent price move cut the land value by about 23 percent.

This is gearing. Land is a thin slice at the bottom of a large stack, so every percentage move in the large numbers becomes a multiple of that move in the small one. It is the same arithmetic that makes leverage amplify returns, applied to price.

CaseLeft for landLand valueChange
Base2,800,0002,718,000none
Costs up 10 percent1,782,0001,730,000about minus 36 percent
Price down 5 percent2,152,0002,089,000about minus 23 percent

Step five: reconcile with the market

A residual is a model, and models carry your assumptions. So finish by comparing it with the market in two ways. First, convert it into a land cost per buildable unit: 2,718,000 divided by 40 units is about 68,000 dollars a unit, or about 680 dollars per square metre of gross floor area. Compare those rates with recent land sales of similar zoning. Second, look at the gap. If comparable sites are trading at 90,000 dollars a unit, either other buyers expect higher prices or lower costs than you, or they are overpaying. Find out which before you raise your offer. If your residual is far above the comparables, be even more suspicious: you have probably left something out, and the most common omissions are finance, sales costs and a realistic contingency. The residual and the comparables should argue with each other. The argument is where you learn what the market believes.

The biggest risk

Offering the base-case residual. If you pay 2.72 million and costs rise 10 percent, you have paid a million dollars more than the land was worth, and that million comes out of your profit, dollar for dollar. The control: offer at or near the downside residual, and justify any premium above it in writing with a specific reason, such as an approval already in hand or a cost already fixed by a contract.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving finance and acquisition costs out. They look small beside the hard cost, but here they total about 580,000 dollars, which is over a fifth of the land value. A residual that ignores them overpays by that amount before anything goes wrong.

Callback

In Week 10 you met yield on cost and the development spread: the gap between what a project yields on its cost and what the market cap rate is. The residual is the same idea solved for a different unknown. There you fixed the land price and asked what return was left; here you fix the return and ask what land price is left. Learn to move between the two and you can check any broker's price in ten minutes.

Recap

Build the project on paper, apply sale price to saleable area and cost to gross area, include sales costs, finance and acquisition costs, take the profit the market demands, and what remains is the land. Then run the downside, because land swings far more than the inputs that drive it. Next: Pax in The Room, a due diligence call with a seller's broker who wants you to waive conditions early.
checklist: Convert units to saleable area before applying sale price
Divide saleable area by efficiency to get gross floor area for cost
Include sales costs, finance and acquisition costs in every residual
State the required profit margin and where it comes from
Run a cost-up and a price-down sensitivity on every residual
Offer at or near the downside residual unless a premium is justified in writing
Show the residual table to your lender and partners
head: Field checklist
speak: Residual land value builds the project on paper and sees what is left for the land. In our hypothetical, 40 units of 80 square metres give 3,200 square metres to sell at 5,000 dollars, so the building is worth 16 million. At 80 percent efficiency, that is 4,000 square metres to build at 2,000 dollars, 8 million of hard cost. Add soft costs, contingency and interest and it costs about 10.16 million to build. Take out 640,000 of sales costs and a 2.4 million profit, and 2.8 million is left. After 3 percent acquisition costs, the land is worth about 2.72 million. Now the warning: costs up 10 percent cuts the land value by about 36 percent, and prices down 5 percent cuts it by about 23 percent. Land is a thin slice at the bottom of a large stack, so it swings hardest. Offer near the downside number, not the base.
terms: Gross development value — the total value of the completed project, by sale or capitalised income.
Efficiency ratio — saleable or leasable area divided by gross floor area; the share of what you build that you can sell.
Gearing — the amplifying effect of a thin residual sitting under a large stack, so small input changes cause large changes in the residual.

hostile.q: A seller's broker says: three comparable lots sold for more than your offer. Your residual is just a lowball tactic. Why should my client accept it?
hostile.a: The comparables tell us what other buyers paid; they do not tell us what this site can support at today's costs. Here is the residual line by line, including sales, finance and acquisition costs, and the downside case. If your client can show me a fixed construction price or an approval that removes risk, I will pay for it. Without that, paying the comparable price means I am betting a third of the land value on costs not moving, and I will not make that bet blind.

title: The broker who wants your conditions gone: holding the line in diligence
summary: A seller's broker calls on day 12 of a 45-day conditional period to say another buyer will go firm, and asks you to waive early. Pax walks through the conversation: what to say, what never to say, the question behind the question, and how to stay calm while the clock is used against you.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the most expensive sentence in land buying is "fine, we'll waive." The seller's broker knows it, and the whole conversation in this lesson is designed to get it out of you. Your job is to make the deal possible without making that mistake.

Recall

Q. In the Millennium Tower case, what was the root cause Ford identified?

A. A boundary problem: the risk sat between two sites and two owners, and nobody was paid to own the interaction between the tower's foundation and the excavation next door.

Q. When a hotel operator pitches you a management agreement, what is the question behind the question?

A. Usually who carries the downside. Fees on revenue pay the operator whether or not you profit, so you ask how much of their fee is at risk on performance.

Q. In a tax conversation, what should you never say about structure?

A. Anything that frames the goal as hiding or avoiding tax rather than structuring for a genuine commercial purpose. Words create evidence of purpose.

Why this matters

Conditional periods are where the seller's leverage is highest and yours is lowest, because you have spent money on reports, you have told your lender and partners about the site, and you want it. A broker's best tool is your sunk cost. When you run your own projects there is no investment committee to say no for you, so you must be able to say it calmly yourself, on the phone, at 7 in the evening, after a night shift.

The scene

This is a composite example. Day 12 of a 45-day conditional period on a 2,000 square metre lot. Your Phase I came back two days ago recommending sampling near an old fuel storage area; the Phase II is booked for next week. Your geotechnical desk study is due in ten days. The broker calls.

Broker: "I'll be straight with you. We have a second buyer ready to go firm, no conditions, at your price. My client likes you and wants to deal with you, but he needs you to waive by Friday. Can you do that?"

Pause before you answer. Two seconds of silence costs nothing and stops you answering the urgency instead of the question.

The lines to say

  • "Thank you for telling me. I want this site, and I'm going to show you how we can close quickly without me buying something I haven't checked."
  • "Here's where I am. The Phase I recommended sampling near the old fuel area. Sampling is booked for Tuesday, results by the following Monday. Geotechnical is due on the 22nd."
  • "I can waive the financing condition now, today, in writing. That's a real commitment. I'll waive environmental and geotechnical the day the reports are in, if they're clean."
  • "If your client wants certainty sooner, I'll increase the deposit on waiver of financing. What I won't do is waive environmental before sampling."
  • "If the other buyer is genuinely firm at this price with no conditions, your client should probably take it. I'd rather lose the site than buy it blind."

Notice what those lines do. They give real things, a waived condition and money, in exchange for time, and they keep the one thing that protects you. They also name your walk-away calmly, which tells the broker you are not bluffing.

Say that out loud now.

"I can give you speed and money. I can't give you blind."

The lines never to say

  • "We really need this site." That tells them your reservation price is high.
  • "The reports are basically a formality." Then why are you paying for them?
  • "Let me see what I can do about the environmental." You have just signalled it is negotiable.
  • "Who's the other buyer?" They will not tell you, and asking shows that the claim has rattled you.
  • Anything that commits you on the phone. Say, "I'll confirm in writing by 10 tomorrow," and do it.

The question behind the question

"Can you waive by Friday?" is rarely about Friday. It is usually one of three things. The seller may have a cash need and a deadline of his own; then a larger deposit or an earlier closing date solves his problem better than your waiver. The broker may want to close the file and get paid; then a clear timetable in writing reassures him. Or there really is another buyer; then the question is whether that buyer's price is truly unconditional, which you can test by offering a modest premium for an extension instead of a waiver.

Worked example, hypothetical numbers. Your deposit is 50,000 dollars, refundable until waiver. You offer to raise it to 150,000 dollars on waiver of financing, with 50,000 dollars of that becoming non-refundable now in exchange for 14 more days on environmental and geotechnical. You put 50,000 dollars at genuine risk to keep conditions protecting a 2.6 million dollar purchase and a possible 600,000 dollar clean-up. That is a trade a careful developer makes; waiving blind is not. Professional sign-off required: your real estate lawyer drafts the amendment.

When to stay silent

After you state your position, stop. The urge to fill silence with justification is how people talk themselves into concessions. If the broker says, "That's not going to work," reply, "Understood. What would your client need to see?" and then wait. Silence on the phone feels long; it is usually less than five seconds.

Holding your state

These calls often come when you are tired. You know from Week 4 that sleep loss after a night shift degrades judgement and makes you more impulsive. A practitioner habit worth keeping: never agree to a material change in a conditional period on the same call. If you are parked and not driving, two or three slow breaths with a longer exhale before you respond can help you sound settled; check with your doctor if you have any breathing or heart condition. Then use the line that buys time honestly: "I'll come back to you in writing by 10 tomorrow."

How the best do it

Large institutional developers rarely have one person who can waive a condition alone. Waivers go through an internal gate: a diligence checklist with every stream signed by the responsible professional, and an investment committee approval recorded before the buyer goes firm. The practice a small developer can copy is the gate, not the committee. Write your own waiver checklist, and make yourself sign it before you sign the waiver, even if you are the only person in the room. It turns a phone call into a process.

The biggest risk

Waiving because of a deadline you did not verify. The control: before any waiver, every diligence stream has a written finding, every finding is priced, and the waiver checklist is signed. If that cannot be done by the deadline, you trade money or another condition for time, or you walk.

The beginner's mistake

Treating "another buyer" as a fact. It may be true. It may be a tactic. Your decision should not depend on which, because your answer is the same either way: here is what I can give, here is what I will not give, and here is when you will have it in writing.

Callback

In Week 3, Kema taught loss aversion: people feel a loss more sharply than an equal gain. The broker's call is built to make you feel the loss of the site. Name that feeling to yourself, then remember the bigger loss is the clean-up bill you would own if you waived blind.

Recap

Pause, give speed and money, keep the protection, name your walk-away, stop talking, and confirm in writing. Ask what the seller really needs and solve that instead of waiving. Use a signed waiver checklist so a tired phone call cannot override your process. Next: Kema closes the week with six questions, a Red Pen drill and the boardroom summary.
checklist: Pause before answering any request to waive
Offer concessions that buy time: waive financing, raise the deposit, shorten closing
Never waive environmental or geotechnical before the reports are in
Ask what the seller actually needs rather than accepting the deadline
Never agree a material change on the same call
Confirm every position in writing by a stated time
Sign your own waiver checklist before signing any waiver
Name your walk-away calmly and mean it
head: Field checklist
speak: A seller's broker calls on day 12 of a 45-day conditional period: another buyer will go firm, can you waive by Friday? Pause first. Then give real things in exchange for time. Waive financing today if you can, raise the deposit, offer a quicker close. Keep the conditions that protect you, environmental and geotechnical, until the reports are in. Say it plainly: I can give you speed and money, I cannot give you blind. Never say you really need the site, never call the reports a formality, never agree a material change on the same call. Ask what the seller actually needs; usually it is cash or certainty, which a bigger deposit can solve. If you are tired after a shift, do not decide on the phone. Say you will confirm in writing by 10 tomorrow, and do. And sign your own waiver checklist before you sign any waiver, even if you are the only one in the room.
terms: Waiver — giving up a condition in writing so the purchase becomes firm and binding.
Reservation price — the most you are prepared to pay, or the least you will accept, before walking away.
Sunk cost — money or effort already spent that cannot be recovered and should not drive the next decision.

hostile.q: The broker says: if you won't waive, you're not a serious buyer. Serious buyers go firm. Why should my client wait for you?
hostile.a: Because a serious buyer is one who closes, and I close on what I have checked. I am waiving financing today and raising the deposit to 150,000, with part of it non-refundable now, so your client has real money and a real commitment. Environmental sampling results are due on a fixed date, and I will waive the day they are clean. If your client has an unconditional offer at this price, he should take it. If he wants a buyer who will still be at the table on closing day, that is me.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 31 review: highest and best use, diligence and the residual
summary: Kema tests the week with six questions, recaps site selection and desk diligence, runs a Red Pen drill on a flawed diligence memo, and closes with a two-minute boardroom explanation and a model answer.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week reduces to one discipline: prove what the land can become, prove what it will cost to get there, and pay only what is left. Today you test whether you can do it from memory and under pressure.

Recall

Q. What are the three commercial outcomes of any adverse diligence finding?

A. Reprice the land, hold back money in a reserve, or walk. Saying nothing means you absorb the cost yourself.

Q. In one sentence, why do mixed-use buildings complicate valuation?

A. Each component has its own income pattern, risk and yield, so the parts must be valued separately and the shared costs allocated before they are added up.

Q. What is the difference between value-added tax and a transfer tax on a property sale?

A. A transfer tax is charged on the transfer of the property itself, usually to the buyer. Value-added or goods and services tax is a tax on supplies that may or may not apply to a given property sale, often with credits for registered businesses. Verify against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Diligence knowledge is useless unless you can produce it when a broker is pushing, a lender is questioning and a partner is impatient. Retrieval practice, answering from memory rather than rereading, is one of the better-supported study methods in learning research. So answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Why are the four tests of highest and best use applied in a fixed order?

Answer: Because legal and physical tests eliminate buildings that cannot exist before you spend effort modelling them. Financial analysis only on buildings that can be built and approved keeps the numbers honest.

Question 2. State the residual land value formula and its two most commonly forgotten costs.

Answer: Gross development value minus total development cost excluding land minus required profit, with acquisition costs taken out of what remains. The two most often forgotten are finance costs and sales costs.

Question 3. Why does the land value swing so much more than construction cost?

Answer: Because land is a thin residual at the bottom of a large stack. In this week's hypothetical, a 10 percent rise in costs cut land value by about 36 percent. That is gearing.

Question 4. What does a Phase I environmental site assessment do, and what does it not do?

Answer: It screens records, history and site observations to identify potential concerns. It does not sample soil or groundwater, so it cannot prove the land is clean; a Phase II does the sampling.

Question 5. Why might a seller's consultant report fail to protect you?

Answer: Because the consultant's duty runs to the client who engaged them. Without a reliance letter you may have no claim if the report is wrong. Get reliance or commission your own.

Question 6. What was Rule 31?

Answer: Know what is under the ground and what will be dug next to it before you own the site, and give the risk between two sites a named owner in writing.

Say that out loud now.

Say Rule 31 without looking, then say the residual formula, then say the three outcomes of a finding.

Recap of the week

Day 1, Pax: highest and best use, the four tests in order, the residual as your price ceiling, and four streams of desk diligence. Day 2, Ford: Millennium Tower, a risk that sat between two sites, and why neighbours and long-term ground behaviour belong in diligence. Day 3, Roman: diligence as a priced option, findings converted to price, reserve or walk, and what the lender does with your file. Day 4, LEX: buyer beware, the contract tools that move risk, environmental owner liability, reliance, and a Canada and Guyana comparison. Day 5, Sage: a full residual worked line by line with sensitivities. Day 6, Pax: holding the line when a broker asks you to waive early.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical memo and find the defects before reading on.

Diligence summary, Lot A, hypothetical. Title: clear, per the seller's lawyer's letter. Environmental: seller's Phase I from nine years ago attached, no further work needed. Geotechnical: the building next door has a basement, so ground conditions are fine. Neighbours: not reviewed. Residual land value: gross development value 16,000,000, minus hard cost 8,000,000, minus soft cost 1,200,000, minus profit 2,400,000, equals 4,400,000. Asking price 4,000,000, so the deal works with 400,000 to spare. Recommendation: waive all conditions Friday to beat the other buyer.

The defects, revealed:

  1. Title from the seller's lawyer. Your own lawyer must search and report; a letter from the other side's counsel is not your evidence.
  2. A nine-year-old Phase I from the seller. It is stale, it was commissioned for someone else, and there is no reliance letter. Site use may have changed since.
  3. Geotechnical by inference. A neighbour's basement says nothing reliable about your soil. It may even signal dewatering risk. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineering.
  4. Neighbours not reviewed. Rule 31, broken in one line.
  5. The residual is missing contingency, finance, sales costs and acquisition costs. Put them back with this week's figures and the 4.4 million becomes about 2.72 million.
  6. Base case only. No downside, so the "400,000 to spare" is fiction.
  7. Waive to beat another buyer. A deadline driving the decision, with no findings priced.

Boardroom drill

Set a two-minute timer and explain this week to an imaginary investment committee. Then compare with the model.

Model answer: "Before we price any site, we establish what it can become: legally permitted, physically buildable, financially feasible and, of those, the most valuable. We then build the project on paper and work backward. Completed value, minus every cost to build including finance and sales, minus the profit the risk requires, leaves the most we can pay for land. Because land sits at the bottom of the stack, it moves hardest: a 10 percent cost rise can remove a third of its value, so we offer near the downside. During the conditional period we run legal, tax, environmental and geotechnical diligence with our own consultants and reliance on every report, and we review the neighbours' plans. Every finding becomes a price change, a holdback or a walk. We do not waive a condition until every stream is in writing and priced."

Score yourself

Mark your boardroom attempt against four tests, each out of 5. Accuracy: did every number and term match this week's lessons, with no invented figures? Structure: did you open with the bottom line, then give the method, then the controls? Composure: did you pause instead of filling silence with "um"? The hard question: did you say what happens when a finding cannot be priced, which is that you walk? A score below 3 on any line tells you which lesson to reread, and rereading is only for the line that scored low. Then answer the hostile question below in your own words, out loud, before reading the model answer. Two short attempts spaced across the week will do more for you than one long session tonight.

The biggest risk

Knowing all of this and still skipping a step when you are tired or eager. The control is the signed waiver checklist from Day 6, used every time, on every site.

The beginner's mistake

Reviewing by rereading. It feels productive and builds false confidence. Close the lesson and answer aloud; the struggle to recall is what makes it stick.

Callback

In Week 6 you practised the hostile question: acknowledge, bridge, answer. The boardroom drill is that skill applied to a week of content. If a committee member interrupts with "what if the soil is bad?", acknowledge it, bridge to the geotechnical condition, and answer with the price, reserve or walk logic.

Recap

Highest and best use sets what the land can become; the residual sets what you can pay; diligence proves both; the contract and the conditional period decide who carries what you miss. Next week Pax returns with REGA on entitlements: the zoning envelope, pre-application meetings, conditions, variances, appeals and development agreements.

head: The six questions
speak: This week in one breath. First, establish what the land can become: legally permitted, physically buildable, financially feasible, and of those the most valuable. That is highest and best use. Second, work backward to the land price: completed value, minus every cost to build including finance and sales costs, minus the profit the risk requires, minus acquisition costs. That residual is your ceiling, and because land sits at the bottom of the stack it swings hardest, so offer near the downside. Third, run desk diligence in four streams, legal, tax, environmental and geotechnical, with your own consultants and reliance on every report, and look at what the neighbours plan to dig. Every finding becomes a price change, a holdback or a walk. The default rule is buyer beware, so protection comes from conditions you control. And never waive a condition until every stream is in writing and priced. Rule 31: know the ground and the neighbours before you own the site.
terms: Retrieval practice — recalling information from memory rather than rereading it, a study method with good research support.
Waiver checklist — a personal, signed list confirming every diligence stream is reported and priced before any condition is waived.
Stale report — a report old enough, or commissioned for someone else, that its findings cannot be relied on for today's decision.

hostile.q: An equity partner asks: you walked away from three sites this year on diligence. Are you too cautious to ever buy anything?
hostile.a: Walking from three sites cost us their diligence fees, which together are a small fraction of one bad clean-up or one overpaid land price. Each walk was a specific finding that could not be priced or contained, and each is documented. The test of the process is not how many sites we buy, it is whether the sites we buy perform. I would rather show you three cheap walks than one expensive mistake, and the pipeline is built to replace them.
